UK.rule: Montreal Convention baggage liability, as applied by UK carriers (CAA guidance)
UK.complaint_deadlines: Contact the airline in writing within seven days for lost or stolen items, or damaged baggage; within 21 days for delayed bags, counted from receiving the delayed bag.
UK.liability_limit: No fixed statutory UK figure is quoted by the CAA beyond the Convention limit; the CAA states the maximum will be "around £1000", though it would be rare to receive this much — actual payout depends on proven value of contents.

EU.rule: Montreal Convention (Regulation (EC) No 2027/97 as amended by Regulation (EC) No 889/2002, giving the Convention force in EU law)
EU.complaint_deadlines: Written complaint to the carrier within 7 days of receipt for damaged baggage, and within 21 days of the date the baggage was placed at the passenger's disposal for delayed baggage.
EU.liability_limit: Montreal Convention Article 22(2) liability for destruction, loss, damage or delay of baggage is currently 1,519 Special Drawing Rights (SDR) per passenger, the figure most recently adjusted by ICAO for inflation (confirmed via the current US DOT baggage-liability page, which tracks the same treaty limit); a passenger can secure a higher limit by making a special declaration of value at check-in and paying a supplementary fee.

US.rule: DOT domestic baggage liability regulation (14 CFR 254) and the Montreal Convention for international flights
US.domestic_liability_limit: "The maximum liability amount allowed by the regulation is $4,700 per passenger" for lost, damaged or delayed bags on domestic flights; airlines may pay more but are not required to.
US.international_liability_limit: For most international flights, the Montreal Convention applies: "The maximum baggage liability for flights covered by the Montreal Convention is currently 1,519 Special Drawing Rights (approximately $2,175.00 US) per passenger."
US.fee_refund_rule: A bag fee must be refunded if the bag is declared lost, or is "significantly delayed" — not delivered within 12 hours of a domestic flight's arrival (15 hours for international flights of 12 hours or less; 30 hours for longer international flights) — provided a mishandled baggage report was filed.

evidence: Property Irregularity Report (PIR) filed at the airport

UK.rule: Tenancy Deposit Protection (Housing Act 2004 Part 6 Chapter 4, as amended) — England and Wales assured shorthold tenancies starting after 6 April 2007
UK.protection_deadline: The landlord (or letting agent) must put the deposit in a government-backed tenancy deposit protection (TDP) scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
UK.return_deadline: The deposit must be returned to the tenant within 10 days of landlord and tenant agreeing how much they'll get back.
UK.penalty_for_not_protecting: Under Housing Act 2004 s.214 (as amended), if the landlord failed to protect the deposit or give the required prescribed information, a court must order the landlord to pay the tenant a sum "not less than the amount of the deposit and not more than three times the amount of the deposit", within 14 days of the court order.
UK.dispute_route: If the deposit is protected in an 'insured' scheme and there's a dispute, the landlord/agent must give the deposit to the TDP scheme, which holds it until the dispute is settled via the scheme's free alternative dispute resolution service.

US.rule: State landlord-tenant statutes (no federal deposit-return deadline); small claims court is the standard enforcement route in every state for amounts within that state's small-claims limit.

Alabama.penalty: A landlord who fails to mail a timely refund/accounting must pay the tenant double the amount of the original deposit.

Alaska.deadline: 30 days after termination when deductions are claimed.

Arizona.deadline: 14 days (excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays) after termination, delivery of possession, and tenant demand.
Arizona.penalty: Tenant may recover the deposit due plus damages equal to twice the amount wrongfully withheld.

Arkansas.deadline: 60 days after tenant moves out (statute applies only to landlords with 6+ units or who employ a property manager).
Arkansas.penalty: Landlord may forfeit the right to withhold any portion; tenant may be entitled to twice the deposit plus costs/attorney's fees.

California.penalty: Landlord who fails to provide the itemized statement may lose the right to claim deductions; bad-faith retention entitles the tenant to up to twice the wrongfully withheld amount.

Colorado.deadline: 30 days after lease termination or surrender of premises, whichever is later, unless the lease specifies longer (max 60 days).
Colorado.penalty: No penalty specified beyond the requirement to provide an itemized statement.

Connecticut.deadline: 21 days after tenancy ends, or 15 days after landlord receives tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later.
Connecticut.penalty: Tenant may recover twice the wrongfully withheld amount as damages.

Delaware.deadline: 20 days after termination/expiration of the rental agreement.
Delaware.penalty: Tenant can seek a full refund plus double that amount as damages.

Florida.deadline: 15 days to return in full if no claim is made; 30 days to send notice of claim by certified mail or email.
Florida.penalty: Landlord who misses the 30-day notice deadline forfeits the right to impose a claim on the deposit.

Hawaii.deadline: 14 days after termination of the rental agreement.
Hawaii.penalty: Landlord who misses the deadline forfeits the right to retain any part of the deposit and must return it in full.

Idaho.deadline: 21 days by default, 30 days maximum, after surrender of premises.

Illinois.deadline: 30 days to furnish an itemized statement; 45 days to return the deposit in full if no itemized statement is given.
Illinois.penalty: A landlord found to have acted in bad faith is liable for twice the deposit plus court costs and attorney's fees.

Iowa.deadline: 30 days from termination and receipt of the tenant's mailing address.
Iowa.penalty: Bad-faith retention subjects the landlord to punitive damages up to twice the monthly rent, plus actual damages.

Kansas.deadline: 14 days after the amount of deductions is determined, but never more than 30 days after termination/possession/tenant demand.
Kansas.penalty: Tenant may recover the amount due plus damages equal to 1.5 times the amount wrongfully withheld.

Kentucky.deadline: No single fixed number of days found; the statute describes a 30-day minimum hold and a 60-day tenant response window after the landlord sends notice of a refund due.

Louisiana.deadline: One month after lease termination (an itemized statement may extend this a further 15 days under a 2026 amendment).

Maine.deadline: 21 days for a tenancy-at-will; 30 days for a written rental agreement.
Maine.penalty: Landlord who misses the deadline forfeits the right to withhold any portion of the deposit.

Maryland.deadline: 45 days after the end of tenancy.
Maryland.penalty: Tenant may recover up to 3 times the wrongfully withheld amount plus reasonable attorney's fees.

Massachusetts.penalty: A landlord who fails to comply and is taken to court must pay triple damages, interest, costs and attorney's fees.

Michigan.deadline: 30 days after termination of occupancy to mail an itemized notice of damages.
Michigan.penalty: No penalty specified by statute; the tenant must respond within 7 days of the itemized notice or forfeit the claimed amount.

Minnesota.deadline: 21 days (3 weeks) after termination of tenancy.
Minnesota.penalty: Landlord who fails to provide the written statement is liable for the withheld portion plus interest as a penalty, in addition to the amount wrongfully withheld.

Missouri.penalty: Tenant may recover twice the amount wrongfully withheld.

Montana.deadline: 10 days after termination if no deductions are claimed; 30 days if deductions are claimed (written itemized list required).
Montana.penalty: Landlord liable for up to twice the deposit for noncompliance.

Nebraska.penalty: If willful and not in good faith, the tenant may recover one month's rent or twice the deposit, whichever is less, plus court costs and attorney fees.

Nevada.penalty: Landlord liable for the entire deposit amount, plus a court-set sum up to the deposit amount, plus costs/fees.

New Hampshire.penalty: Landlord liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld.

New Jersey.deadline: 30 days after tenancy ends (5 days if the tenant was displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation).
New Jersey.penalty: A court may award double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus full costs and, at the court's discretion, attorney's fees; the landlord forfeits the right to deduct if no itemized statement is sent within 30 days.

New Mexico.deadline: 30 days after termination of the rental agreement or departure, whichever is later.
New Mexico.penalty: Landlord who misses the deadline forfeits the right to withhold any portion and loses the right to counterclaim, and is liable for the tenant's court costs/attorney fees; bad-faith retention carries a separate $250 statutory civil penalty (NMSA 47-8-18).

New York.penalty: Landlord forfeits any right to retain any portion of the deposit if the 14-day deadline is missed.

North Carolina.deadline: 30 days after termination/delivery of possession for an interim accounting; final accounting within 60 days if the amount can't be determined by day 30.
North Carolina.penalty: No separate penalty specified; the statute instead requires the interim and final accounting deadlines described above.

North Dakota.deadline: 30 days after termination of lease and delivery of possession.
North Dakota.penalty: A landlord who withholds without justification is liable for triple the amount withheld.

Ohio.deadline: 30 days after termination of the rental agreement and delivery of possession.
Ohio.penalty: Tenant may recover the deposit plus damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld, plus reasonable attorney's fees.

Oklahoma.deadline: 45 days after termination, delivery of possession, and written tenant demand (30 days for undamaged furnished-rental deposits).
Oklahoma.penalty: No penalty figure specified; the deposit reverts to the landlord if the tenant doesn't demand it within 6 months.

Oregon.deadline: 31 days after the tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession.
Oregon.penalty: Tenant may recover twice the amount withheld without a required written accounting, or withheld in bad faith (ORS 90.300).

Pennsylvania.deadline: 30 days after the tenant moves out.
Pennsylvania.penalty: Landlord liable for double the amount by which the deposit exceeds actual damages, if the 30-day deadline is missed (68 P.S. Section 250.512).

Rhode Island.deadline: 20 days after the later of termination, delivery of possession, or the tenant providing a forwarding address.
Rhode Island.penalty: Tenant may recover the amount due plus damages equal to twice the amount wrongfully withheld, plus attorney fees.

South Carolina.deadline: 30 days after termination, delivery of possession, and tenant demand, whichever is later.
South Carolina.penalty: Tenant may recover the property/money plus damages equal to three times the amount wrongfully withheld, plus attorney's fees.

South Dakota.deadline: 21 days after termination of tenancy and receipt of the tenant's mailing address (itemized accounting within 45 days on request).
South Dakota.penalty: Landlord forfeits all rights to withhold any portion; bad-faith retention subjects the landlord to punitive damages up to $200.

Tennessee.deadline: No single fixed statutory deadline found; the law requires inspection within 3 working days of move-out and a damage listing, with a 60-day window for the tenant to respond to a refund notice before the landlord may retain unclaimed funds.
Tennessee.penalty: Landlord forfeits the right to retain any portion if the deposit wasn't held in a separate account and a damage listing wasn't provided as required.

Texas.deadline: 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises.
Texas.penalty: No penalty figure quoted; Property Code Chapter 92 Subchapter C provides a bad-faith-retention penalty provision.

Utah.deadline: 30 days after the renter vacates and returns possession.

Vermont.deadline: 14 days from when the landlord discovers/learns the tenant vacated (60 days for seasonal rentals).
Vermont.penalty: Landlord forfeits the right to withhold any portion if missed; if willful, liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees/costs.

Virginia.deadline: 45 days after termination/the tenant vacates, whichever is later.
Virginia.penalty: If willful noncompliance is found, a court orders return of the deposit plus actual damages and reasonable attorney fees.

Washington.deadline: 30 days after termination and vacation of the premises (the deadline has changed over time — was 14 days, then 21 days, now 30 days under current RCW 59.18.280).
Washington.penalty: Landlord liable to the tenant for the full amount of the deposit if the deadline/statement requirement is missed.

West Virginia.deadline: Statute references delivery "within the applicable notice period" (not a single flat number), with a further 15-day extension for itemizing damage requiring a third-party contractor.
West Virginia.penalty: If willful/bad faith, the tenant is entitled to judgment for the unreturned deposit plus damages equal to 1.5 times the amount wrongfully withheld.

Wisconsin.deadline: 21 days after the tenant moves out (or from the last day of the lease/new tenant move-in, whichever is first, for early move-outs).
Wisconsin.penalty: Tenant may recover twice the amount of actual pecuniary loss, plus court costs and, if awarded, attorney fees.

Wyoming.deadline: 30 days after termination of the rental agreement, or 15 days after receipt of the renter's new address, whichever is later (extended to 60 days total if there's damage).

District of Columbia.deadline: 45 days to return the deposit with interest or notify of withholding; a further 30 days to provide an itemized statement if withholding.
District of Columbia.penalty: No penalty figure specified by statute.

US.small_claims_route: If a landlord doesn't return the deposit or an itemized deduction statement within the state deadline, tenants in every state can sue in their local small claims court; limits and procedures vary by state.

evidence: Proof of deposit payment and protection certificate

UK.what_is_unlawful: It is a criminal offence to unlawfully deprive a residential occupier of occupation of the premises (or any part), or to attempt to, unless the person believed (with reasonable cause) that the occupier had ceased to reside there. It is also an offence for a landlord or their agent, with intent to cause the occupier to leave or stop exercising a right, to do acts likely to interfere with their peace or comfort, or to persistently withdraw/withhold services reasonably required for occupying the premises (e.g. cutting off utilities).
UK.penalties: On summary conviction: a fine and/or up to 6 months' imprisonment. On conviction on indictment: an unlimited fine and/or up to 2 years' imprisonment.
UK.who_to_contact: "Contact the police if physical violence or threats are involved or if someone is trying to remove you or your belongings from the property without either a court order or court appointed bailiff." For non-emergencies: "Talk to your local council if you think you're being harassed or threatened with illegal eviction." Also: a legal adviser, Citizens Advice, or Shelter's housing advice helpline.
UK.remedies: A tenant may be able to "be let back into your home", "claim compensation", or "apply for a rent repayment order"; local councils can take legal action if there's enough evidence of harassment or illegal eviction.

US.rule: No single federal statute bans self-help eviction for private tenancies generally — eviction procedure is governed by state/local landlord-tenant law, which in nearly all states requires a court order before a tenant can be removed or locked out. A specific federal rule exists for HUD-assisted housing.
US.hud_assisted_housing_rule: For HUD-assisted housing, HUD prohibits lease clauses that would let an owner/PHA evict a tenant or seize/sell belongings without legal proceedings, or turn off utilities to force a tenant out; "an owner must not evict any tenant except by judicial action pursuant to state and local laws."
US.general_private_tenancies: Self-help eviction (lockouts, utility shutoffs, removing belongings without a court order) is illegal in the large majority of states under their own landlord-tenant statutes, but the specific penalty and procedure vary by state — check the tenant's specific state statute.

evidence: Dated record of lockout or utility cut-off

UK.rule: Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.11, Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018, and (for social housing) Awaab's Law
UK.s11_duty: Section 11 implies a covenant that the landlord will keep in repair the structure and exterior of the dwelling (including drains, gutters, external pipes), and keep in repair and proper working order the installations for water, gas, electricity, sanitation, and space/water heating — subject to exceptions (e.g. tenant's own tenant-like-use damage, destruction by fire/flood/tempest).
UK.hfhha_2018: The Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018 requires rented homes in England to be 'fit for human habitation' (safe, healthy, free from serious hazards e.g. damp/mould, structural problems, inadequate heating, carbon monoxide, electrical/fire hazards). If not, the tenant can take the landlord to court, which can order repairs and/or compensation. Applies immediately to tenancies signed on or after 20 March 2019; tenancies signed before that date were covered from 20 March 2020 (or sooner if a new tenancy/rolling contract started).
UK.awaabs_law_status: In force for the SOCIAL rented sector only, from 27 October 2025: social landlords must fix emergency health/safety hazards within 24 hours of reporting, investigate significant damp/mould within 10 working days and make the property safe within 5 working days, and report inspection findings to the tenant within 3 working days. From 30 November 2026 this is due to expand to further hazards (excess cold/heat, falls, structural collapse, fire/explosion, electrical hazards, domestic hygiene). Does not currently apply to private rented tenancies.
UK.council_route: Tenants of private landlords can report serious hazards to the council's environmental health team, which can assess the property under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS) and require the landlord to make repairs.

US.rule: No single federal implied warranty of habitability for private rentals — this is a state common-law/statutory doctrine that varies by state; HUD only sets specific repair/habitability rules for HUD-assisted housing.
US.general_principle: Most states recognize an implied warranty of habitability requiring landlords to maintain rental housing in a livable condition, and many states allow tenants a 'repair and deduct' remedy (paying for the repair and deducting the cost from rent, usually within statutory dollar/frequency limits) or rent withholding/escrow — but the existence, procedure, and limits of these remedies vary by state statute, so the tenant should check their specific state's landlord-tenant law.
US.hud_assisted_housing_only: For HUD-assisted housing specifically, HUD sets its own resident rights to timely repairs and a quality maintenance program under the applicable HUD occupancy handbook/lease requirements.

UK.rule: Housing Act 1988 s.13 ('section 13 process'), as applied to assured periodic tenancies under the regime in force since the Renters' Rights Act 2025 reforms commenced on 1 May 2026
UK.when_and_how: A landlord can only increase the rent once a year, and cannot increase it in the first year of the tenancy. The landlord must give at least 2 months' notice using form 4A ('Landlord's notice proposing a new rent'), delivered in person, by post, or by email if the tenancy agreement allows it.
UK.tribunal_challenge: If the tenant thinks the proposed increase is higher than the 'open market rent' (what the landlord could expect letting the property afresh on the open market), they can ask the First-tier Tribunal to review it.
UK.transitional_rule: Rent review clauses in tenancy agreements can no longer be used for rent increases taking effect after 1 May 2026, even if agreed before that date. If notice was given using the old 'form 4' before 1 May 2026, its notice period/increase still applies even if the new rent starts after that date, and the tenant can still challenge it at the Tribunal. After any increase (via form 4 or a rent review clause), the next increase cannot take effect until at least a year after the last one did.

US.rule: No federal law on rent increase notice periods or rent control — governed entirely by state/local law, which varies widely. Most states have no rent control and simply require the same notice as for ending a periodic tenancy (commonly 30 days, longer in some states/cities).
US.state_examples_verified: California (Tenant Protection Act of 2019 / AB 1482): for most covered rental units, rent increases are capped at 5% plus the regional CPI change, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period, with no more than 2 increases in a 12-month period. Oregon (SB 608 as amended by SB 611): statewide rent increases on most tenancies are capped at 7% plus CPI or 10%, whichever is lower, published annually by the state; landlords must also give 90 days' notice of a rent increase (HB 3113).

evidence: The increase notice with date served

UK.short_term_right_to_reject: A 30-day window from delivery/taking possession of goods that don't conform to the contract, within which the consumer can reject them for a full refund.
UK.six_month_presumption: If the consumer chooses repair, replacement, price reduction or the final right to reject within the first 6 months, the fault is presumed to have been present at delivery unless the trader proves otherwise (or this is inconsistent with the circumstances, e.g. obvious abuse/misuse). No deduction can be made for use where goods are rejected within the first 6 months, except for motor vehicles.
UK.after_six_months: The burden of proof shifts to the consumer to show the defect was present at delivery.

US.rule: No general federal right to return/refund goods — the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act (15 U.S.C. 2301 et seq.) only regulates written warranties where a business chooses to offer one; it does not require a refund or return policy.
US.warranty_rules: Magnuson-Moss does not require any business to provide a written warranty. Where a written warranty is offered, the business cannot disclaim or modify implied warranties, and a 'full warranty' designation entitles the customer to a replacement or refund if repair isn't possible. Remedies otherwise depend on the seller's own return policy and state consumer-protection/UCC implied-warranty law.

EU.rule: Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU (withdrawal right) and Directive (EU) 2019/771 (sale of goods legal guarantee)
EU.withdrawal_right: Article 9(1) of Directive 2011/83/EU: for distance/off-premises contracts, "the consumer shall have a period of 14 days" to withdraw from the contract without giving any reason.
EU.legal_guarantee: Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2019/771 ('Liability of the seller') makes the seller liable where a lack of conformity becomes apparent within two years of delivery (member states may set a longer national period).

US.rule: FTC Negative Option Rule (status uncertain for the 2024 "click-to-cancel" amendments) and ROSCA
US.click_to_cancel_status: The FTC announced a final "click-to-cancel" rule on 16 October 2024 and denied a petition to stay it pending judicial review on 13 December 2024. However, as of 13 March 2026 the FTC's own Negative Option Rule page states the Commission "seeks public comment on the need for amendments to" the rule "to help consumers avoid recurring payments... and allow them to cancel such payments without unwarranted obstacles" — a new Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking. The strict 2024 click-to-cancel provisions are not confirmed to be in full force today.
US.rosca_still_applies: Independent of the above, the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA), a separate federal statute, continues to require clear disclosure of all material terms, express informed consent, and a simple cancellation mechanism for negative-option/recurring online sales.

UK.rule: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (DMCCA) new subscription contracts regime — NOT YET IN FORCE
UK.commencement_status: The government's consultation response (updated 2 April 2026) states: "We will legislate when parliamentary time allows and we anticipate that the regime will commence in spring 2027." As of today, the DMCCA's new subscription-specific rules have not commenced — only the existing Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 (CCRs) currently apply, which already give a 14-day cooling-off right for contracts made at a distance or away from business premises.
UK.future_regime_summary: Once in force, the DMCCA will require: clear pre-contract information; reminder notices before a free/discounted trial or a 12-month+ contract auto-renews; an 'easy exit' — straightforward cancellation, available online if the consumer signed up online; and TWO 14-day cooling-off periods — an 'initial' cooling-off period on entering the contract, and a new 'renewal' cooling-off period after a trial or 12-month+ contract auto-renews, during which the consumer can cancel (for a full or proportionate refund depending on what's been supplied).

EU.cancellation_right: Article 9(1): for distance/off-premises contracts (including subscriptions sold this way), "the consumer shall have a period of 14 days" to withdraw without giving any reason.

US.rule: Fair Credit Billing Act (credit cards) and ROSCA (recurring/negative-option charges generally)
US.fcba_dispute_window: Send a written dispute notice no later than 60 days after the credit card company sent the statement where the error (the post-cancellation charge) first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge and up to two billing cycles to investigate, and the disputed amount doesn't have to be paid while under investigation.
US.rosca: ROSCA requires sellers running recurring/negative-option plans to provide a simple cancellation mechanism; a charge made after a valid cancellation is itself evidence of a ROSCA violation, reportable to the FTC.

UK.rule: Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 / chargeback, plus the right to withdraw consent for a continuous payment authority (CPA) under the Payment Services Regulations 2017
UK.cpa_cancellation_right: Regulation 67 of the Payment Services Regulations 2017: "The payer may withdraw its consent to the execution of a series of payment transactions at any time with the effect that any future payment transactions are not regarded as authorised." In practice, a consumer can cancel a recurring card payment/CPA directly with their own bank or card issuer at any time, regardless of what the merchant says, and the bank must act on it; charges taken after that withdrawal are treated as unauthorised transactions (subject to the same next-business-day refund duty confirmed for unauthorized-transaction.UK in claims-batch1-money.json).
UK.section_75_chargeback: For card purchases over £100 up to £30,000, Section 75 joint liability may also apply; for other amounts, or debit cards, chargeback (120-day window) is the route — see the figures already verified in the 'chargeback' claim.

US.rule: For ACA-compliant individual/group health plans: federal internal appeal / external review rules; for employer self-funded plans: ERISA claims procedure; for other insurance (auto, home, life): state insurance department complaint route.
US.internal_appeal: You must file your internal appeal within 180 days (6 months) of receiving notice that your claim was denied. The insurer must notify you of a denial within 15 days for prior authorization, 30 days for services already received, or 72 hours for urgent care. The internal appeal itself must be completed within 30 days (service not yet received) or 60 days (service already received); for urgent situations, a decision must come within at least 4 business days, with written notice following within 48 hours.
US.external_review: If the internal appeal is denied, you can request an independent external review; the insurer's final determination must explain how to request one.

UK.rule: FCA Handbook ICOBS 8 (Insurers: general) claims-handling rules, plus the Financial Ombudsman Service complaint route
UK.icobs_claims_handling: ICOBS 8.1.1R: an insurer must (1) handle claims promptly and fairly; (2) provide reasonable guidance to help a policyholder make a claim and appropriate information on its progress; (3) not unreasonably reject a claim (including by terminating or avoiding a policy); and (4) settle claims promptly once settlement terms are agreed.
UK.unreasonable_rejection: ICOBS 8.1.2A guidance: rejection is considered unreasonable (among other cases) for a misrepresentation that isn't a 'qualifying misrepresentation', or for breach of warranty/term/fraud where the insurer can't rely on the relevant Insurance Act 2015 provisions.
UK.complaint_route: A business has 8 weeks to consider most complaints (15 days specifically for fraud/scams, payment services, or e-money complaints) before the consumer can refer it to the Financial Ombudsman Service; the consumer then has 6 months from the date of the firm's final response to bring the complaint to the Ombudsman.

US.surprise_billing_protections: Patients are protected from unexpected out-of-network bills for: "Emergency room visits"; "Non-emergency care related to a visit to an in-network hospital, hospital outpatient department, or ambulatory surgical center"; and "Air ambulance services."
US.good_faith_estimate: Uninsured/self-pay patients: "providers must give you a good faith estimate of how much your health care will cost if you request one or schedule services at least 3 business days in advance."
US.dispute_process: "You may be able to dispute your bill if it's at least $400 more than the estimate."

UK.rule: NHS Constitution for England — complaints and redress
UK.nhs_complaint_route: The NHS Constitution gives patients the right to have any complaint dealt with efficiently and properly investigated, and: "You have the right to take your complaint to the independent Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman... if you are not satisfied with the way your complaint has been dealt with by the NHS."

US.response_deadline: "Your doctor normally has up to 30 days to provide you a copy of your information", though it's often provided sooner, especially via a patient web portal.
US.fees: You can't be denied access for not paying your medical bill. Your doctor can charge you a reasonable fee for a copy of your health information; the fee may not be a per-page fee if your information is stored electronically.
US.complaint_route: If you believe your HIPAA access rights were violated, you can file a complaint with the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR).

UK.rule: UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018 — right of access (subject access request, SAR)
UK.response_deadline: "Organisations usually have one month to respond to a SAR." Anyone can make a SAR without needing a solicitor or lawyer.
UK.nhs_route: For NHS medical records specifically, a SAR can be made directly to the relevant NHS organisation/GP practice holding the records, following the same SAR process and 1-month deadline described above.

evidence: Provider details and dates of treatment

US.rule: Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), enforced by the DOL Wage and Hour Division (WHD)
US.minimum_wage_overtime: Federal minimum wage is $7.25 per hour (effective since 24 July 2009); where state and federal minimum wage both apply, the employee is entitled to the higher of the two. Covered nonexempt employees must receive overtime at 1.5x their regular rate of pay for hours worked over 40 in a workweek.
US.limitation_period: "For willful violations, the Department may recover back wages and an equal amount in liquidated damages for a period of up to 3 years."
US.complaint_route: Complaints can be filed with the DOL Wage and Hour Division; state wage laws (minimum wage, payday, and other requirements) vary by state and were not individually verified here.

UK.rule: Employment Rights Act 1996 (ERA 1996) Part II — unlawful deductions from wages — plus the ACAS Early Conciliation requirement before an employment tribunal claim
UK.tribunal_time_limit: Section 23(2) of the Employment Rights Act 1996 states "an employment tribunal shall not consider a complaint under this section unless it is presented before the end of the period of six months beginning with" the date of the deduction. Section 23(4) allows the tribunal to extend this if it wasn't reasonably practicable to present the complaint within that period.
UK.acas_early_conciliation: Before lodging most employment tribunal claims, a claimant must notify Acas, which will offer early conciliation — a voluntary process where an Acas conciliator tries to help reach an agreement without going to tribunal. Notifying Acas does not change the underlying tribunal time limit, though the conciliation period itself can pause ('stop the clock' on) that time limit.
UK.hmrc_minimum_wage: HMRC enforces the National Minimum Wage on behalf of the Fair Work Agency; workers can complain using the online 'Complain about pay and work rights' form, and can report an employer even after leaving the job. A complaint can't be taken forward if the worker has already started tribunal action for the same National Minimum Wage issue.

US.rule: No federal final-paycheck deadline — governed entirely by state law, which varies.

California.quit_deadline: Immediately if the employee gave at least 72 hours' notice and quits on the day stated; otherwise within 72 hours of quitting.
California.fired_deadline: Immediately at the time of termination.
California.vacation_payout: Accrued unused vacation must be paid out in all separation scenarios.

Arizona.quit_deadline: No later than the regular payday for the pay period during which the termination occurred.
Arizona.fired_deadline: Within seven working days or the end of the next regular pay period, whichever is sooner.

Minnesota.quit_deadline: Not later than the first regularly scheduled payday following the employee's final day of employment (may extend to the second payday, but never more than 20 calendar days total, if the first payday is fewer than 5 days after termination).
Minnesota.fired_deadline: Immediately due and payable upon the employee's demand; the employer is in default if not paid within 24 hours of demand.

Missouri.quit_deadline: Not specified; the statute addresses discharge (being fired) only — see fired_deadline.
Missouri.fired_deadline: Wages are due on the day of discharge; if not paid within 7 days of the employee's written demand, wages continue accruing at the same rate until paid, up to a maximum of 60 days.

UK.rule: Employment Rights Act 1996 (notice pay) and the statutory holiday entitlement rules (Working Time Regulations 1998, as reflected in current gov.uk guidance)
UK.notice_pay: Statutory minimum notice an employer must give: "at least one week's notice if employed between one month and 2 years; one week's notice for each year if employed between 2 and 12 years; 12 weeks' notice if employed for 12 years or more." An employer may give more than this statutory minimum (per the contract) but not less. The employer should either pay the employee through the notice period or pay in lieu of notice; notice pay is based on the average earned per week over the 12 weeks before the notice period starts.
UK.holiday_pay_on_leaving: "The only time someone can get paid in place of taking statutory leave (known as 'payment in lieu') is when they leave their job. Employers must pay for untaken statutory leave, even if the worker is dismissed for gross misconduct." Statutory leave entitlement is 5.6 weeks (28 days for a worker on a 5-day week) a year.

US.rule: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (enforced by the EEOC)
US.charge_deadline: "In general, you need to file a charge within 180 calendar days from the day the discrimination took place. The 180 calendar day filing deadline is extended to 300 calendar days if a state or local agency enforces a law that prohibits employment discrimination on the same basis." Federal employees must generally contact an agency EEO Counselor within 45 days instead.
US.ongoing_harassment_rule: "In harassment cases, you must file your charge within 180 or 300 days of the last incident of harassment", although the EEOC will look at all incidents of harassment when investigating, even if earlier incidents happened more than 180/300 days earlier.
US.retaliation_protection: "The EEO laws prohibit punishing job applicants or employees for asserting their rights to be free from employment discrimination including harassment" (filing/witnessing a charge, reporting harassment, refusing to participate in discriminatory conduct, resisting sexual advances, etc. are all protected activity). Employer coverage under Title VII requires 15 or more employees; the retaliation charge deadline is the same 180 days (extendable by state law).

UK.rule: Equality Act 2010, section 26 (harassment) and section 123 (time limits)
UK.harassment_definition: Section 26: A harasses B if A engages in unwanted conduct related to a relevant protected characteristic (or of a sexual nature, or related to gender reassignment/sex), and the conduct has the purpose or effect of "violating B's dignity" or "creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment for B" — including where B is treated less favourably because of their rejection of or submission to such conduct. Protected characteristics include age, disability, gender reassignment, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.
UK.tribunal_time_limit: Section 123(1)(a) of the Equality Act 2010 sets the time limit as "the period of 6 months starting with the date of the act to which the complaint relates" (amended from the original 3 months). An employment tribunal may extend this further if it thinks it just and equitable to do so.
UK.acas_early_conciliation: As with other employment tribunal claims, a claimant must notify Acas before bringing most tribunal claims; Acas then offers early conciliation, a voluntary process to try to resolve the dispute before tribunal.

UK.rule: Consumer Rights Act 2015, section 29 (passing of risk), plus Royal Mail's own claims process for lost/damaged/delayed items
UK.seller_responsible_until_delivery: "The goods remain at the trader's risk until they come into the physical possession of— (a) the consumer, or (b) a person identified by the consumer to take possession of the goods." If the consumer independently arranges their own carrier (not one offered or recommended by the trader), the goods become the consumer's responsibility once handed to that carrier instead.
UK.royal_mail_claims_process: Royal Mail runs its own Claims Centre: claimants need digital evidence including proof of posting and proof of value; how and when you can claim depends on the exact service used (e.g. Special Delivery vs other items have different delay-compensation rules) — Royal Mail publishes separate compensation policies for delay, loss, and damage.

US.rule: FTC Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule (16 CFR Part 435) and USPS indemnity claims process
US.ftc_30_day_shipping_rule: "The Rule, issued in 1975, requires sellers who solicit buyers to order merchandise through the mail, via the Internet, or by phone to have a reasonable basis to expect that the sellers can ship within the advertised time frame, or, if no time frame is specified, within 30 days." If the seller can't ship on time, "the seller must obtain the buyer's consent to a delay in shipping or refund payment for the unshipped merchandise."
US.usps_claims: For insured USPS mail (e.g. Priority Mail Express, other insured mail, COD items, insured Registered Mail) that's lost, damaged, or has missing contents, either the sender or recipient can file an indemnity claim; the filing period varies by mail service. USPS usually sends a claims decision within 5-10 days, and approved claims are paid in 7-10 business days (never more than the item's actual value). A denied or partially-paid claim can be appealed within 30 days of the decision, with a second/final appeal available within 30 days of the first appeal's denial.

EU.rule: Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU, Article 20 ('Passing of risk')
EU.seller_liability_until_delivery: "In contracts where the trader dispatches the goods to the consumer, the risk of loss of or damage to" the goods passes to the consumer only once the consumer (or a third party indicated by the consumer, other than the carrier) has acquired physical possession of the goods — mirroring the UK's CRA 2015 s.29 (which implemented this same EU-derived rule domestically). If the consumer arranges their own carrier not offered by the trader, risk passes on handover to that carrier instead.

UK.rule: UK customs/VAT rules for goods sent from abroad (gov.uk guidance)
UK.thresholds: VAT is charged on all goods sent from outside the UK to Great Britain (or from outside the UK/EU to Northern Ireland), except gifts worth £39 or less. Customs Duty applies on non-excise goods worth more than £135 (no charge at or below £135); excise goods (alcohol, tobacco, vapes) are dutiable at any value. For goods worth £135 or less bought directly, the seller should already have included VAT in the price; the delivery company only charges VAT separately for gifts worth over £39 or excise goods.
UK.courier_handling: Royal Mail, Parcelforce or the courier company contacts you with a bill for any VAT/duty/delivery charges owed, and will normally hold the parcel for about 3 weeks before returning it to the sender if unpaid.
UK.how_to_dispute: To get a refund if you were overcharged tax or you return the goods, fill in form BOR286 (if Royal Mail or Parcelforce delivered the goods) or form C285 (for any other courier/freight company).

EU.rule: EU VAT e-commerce reform (in force since 1 July 2021), as described on the European Commission's VAT One Stop Shop site
EU.vat_exemption_removed: "The VAT exemption at importation of small consignments of a value up to EUR 22 is removed. This means all goods imported in the EU are subject to VAT."
EU.ioss_threshold: "The Import One Stop Shop (IOSS) has been created to simplify the declaration and payment of VAT for distance sales of low value goods not exceeding 150€ imported from third territories or third countries." Special arrangements for consignments up to €150 also exist for sellers who don't use the IOSS.

UK.rule: Consumer Rights Act 2015 — applies to dealer (trader) sales only; private sales are governed separately
UK.satisfactory_quality: Section 9: "Every contract to supply goods is to be treated as including a term that the quality of the goods is satisfactory" — judged by what a reasonable person would consider satisfactory, given the description, price, and all other relevant circumstances (including the goods' fitness for normal purpose, appearance/finish, freedom from minor defects, safety, and durability). Does not cover defects specifically pointed out before purchase, or apparent from the buyer's own pre-purchase examination.
UK.short_term_right_and_presumption: Same 30-day short-term right to reject and 6-month reversed-burden-of-proof presumption already confirmed for the 'refund-defective-product' claim apply equally to used cars bought from a dealer.
UK.private_sales: The Consumer Rights Act 2015 only applies to contracts where a trader supplies goods to a consumer — it does not apply to private (person-to-person) sales. For a private sale, the main protection is that the goods must match their description ('as described'); there is no statutory satisfactory-quality or fitness-for-purpose guarantee from a private seller.

US.rule: FTC Used Car Rule (16 CFR Part 455) plus state-level implied warranty and lemon laws
US.used_car_rule: In force since 1985, formally the Used Motor Vehicle Trade Regulation Rule: dealers must display a window sticker, the 'Buyers Guide', disclosing whether the car is sold with a warranty and, if so, its terms (duration, percentage of repair costs covered, which systems are covered). "In states that do not permit sales of used cars 'as is,' or without warranties, dealers must display an alternative version of the Buyers Guide."
US.state_variation: Whether a dealer can sell 'as is' (no warranty), and whether a state's used-car 'lemon law' gives extra protection, varies by state and was not individually verified here.

US.rule: Report to multiple federal agencies depending on the scam type; realistic recovery is limited.
US.where_to_report: FTC: report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov ("We can't resolve your individual report, but we use reports to investigate and bring cases against fraud, scams, and bad business practices."). FBI: report cyber-enabled crime, including crypto scams, to the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at ic3.gov — IC3 "cannot guarantee a response to every complaint" but reports can help identify patterns and, in some cases, help freeze stolen funds. CFTC: if the scam involves commodity/derivatives fraud, report via a Complaint Form or whistleblower Form TCR to the Division of Enforcement (866-366-2382). SEC: if the scam involves an unregistered or fraudulent securities offer (e.g. a fake token sale, Ponzi/pyramid scheme), report via the SEC's online Tips, Complaints, and Referrals (TCR) system.
US.realistic_recovery: None of the above agencies can get your money back for you individually — the FTC and IC3 both state explicitly that they cannot resolve individual reports or guarantee a response; reports are used for investigations and to help law enforcement identify and prosecute scammers.
US.card_bank_reversal: If you paid by credit/debit card, you may be able to dispute the charge (see the FCBA figures already confirmed under 'chargeback'), though cryptocurrency purchases/transfers themselves generally cannot be reversed once confirmed on the blockchain. Beware of 'recovery scams' where fraudsters pose as being able to recover your lost crypto for a fee.

UK.rule: Report Fraud (Action Fraud) / Police Scotland, plus FCA tools for checking firms and reporting unauthorised activity
UK.where_to_report: "Contact Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or via the website... If you live in Scotland, you should report to Police Scotland by calling 101, or contact Advice Direct Scotland on 0808 164 6000." The FCA itself can only look into scams involving financial services it regulates, and explicitly states: "We can't help you get your money back, but we look into every report we receive and it could help protect others."
UK.fca_firm_checker: Use the FCA Firm Checker to find out if a firm is authorised and has permission for the service it's offering — equivalent to checking the FCA's warning list of unauthorised firms. Also beware 'recovery room scammers' who pretend to be legitimate firms offering to recover lost funds.

US.rule: No single federal crypto-exchange regulator — oversight is split, with a general CFPB complaint route for consumer financial products/services
US.cfpb_route: Submit a complaint at consumerfinance.gov/complaint; the CFPB states "most companies respond within 15 days," and will forward the complaint to a different agency if it determines another regulator is better placed to help.

UK.rule: Crypto activity remains largely unregulated in the UK as a matter of financial services regulation, which limits both FCA and Financial Ombudsman protections (only AML/marketing rules for crypto firms are currently regulated)
UK.regulatory_status: The FCA's own current consumer guidance (updated 29/01/2026) states plainly: "crypto is largely unregulated in the UK, so it is highly unlikely you will be covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme" and "as crypto activity is not regulated yet in the UK, there is no safety net if things go wrong." The marketing of crypto is regulated (firms must show prominent risk warnings and can't offer joining/referral bonuses) — use the FCA Firm Checker to see if a firm is on the FCA's register.

EU.in_force_dates: "This Regulation shall apply from 30 December 2024", confirmed directly on the operative text of the regulation (Article 149). Titles III and IV (on asset-referenced tokens/e-money tokens, i.e. stablecoins) applied earlier, from 30 June 2024, 'by way of derogation'. As of today, MiCA is fully in force across all titles.
EU.complaint_handling_duty: MiCA requires issuers of asset-referenced tokens to "put in place a clear procedure for handling complaints received from holders" (recital 49, given effect by the operative Article 31, 'Complaints-handling procedures'); crypto-asset service providers (including exchanges) are subject to equivalent complaints-handling obligations under the Regulation's Title V provisions, which took effect on the same 30 December 2024 general application date.
